description_full: Thomson Reuters Corporation operates as a content and technology company in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia Pacific. It operates through five segments: Legal Professionals, Corporates, Tax, Audit & Accounting Professionals, Reuters News, and Global Print. The Legal Professionals segment offers research and workflow products focusing on legal research and integrated legal workflow solutions that combine content, tools, and analytics to law firms and governments. The Corporates segment provides a suite of content-driven technologies, including generative AI and integrated compliance workflow solutions to small businesses and multinational organizations. Tax, Audit & Accounting Professionals segment offers research and workflow products to tax, audit, and accounting firms. The Reuters News segment provides business, financial, and international news to media organizations, professional, and news consumers through Reuters News Agency, Reuters.com, Reuters Events, Thomson Reuters products, and to financial firms. The Global Print segment offers legal and tax information primarily in print format. The company was formerly known as The Thomson Corporation and changed its name to Thomson Reuters Corporation in April 2008. The company was founded in 1799 and is headquartered in Toronto, Canada. Thomson Reuters Corporation is a subsidiary of The Woodbridge Company Limited.

financial_summary: Thomson Reuters Corp is a large-cap industrials business with a $47.4B market cap on $7.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 8% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $2.0B in free cash flow — roughly 27 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.76× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.7× net debt/EBITDA.

Shareholder yield of 4.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 71% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 29% operating margin runs 20pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.56x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.5% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-9.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 22% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 23% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 52% and a beta of 0.68, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $157.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 35% in the 2020 crash, 21% in the 2022 bear market and 50% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $74.77 (margin of safety -46%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 21%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $60.31 to $94.78 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 33.5 vs 24.1 and EV/EBITDA 21.2 vs 13.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 11% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 13 covering analysts target $128 on average, 17% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 8.1%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.41).
It converts 27% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.76x.
ROE of 13% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.7x net debt to EBITDA ($605.0M of cash against $2.1B of debt).
The current ratio of 0.64 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 44% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.1% over 3 years and 4.6% over 5 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 19%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 10.2% a year over five years.
Analysts expect 18.0% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 71.0%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 29%.
It returns 4.5% a year to shareholders (2.1% in buybacks and 2.4% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 23 consecutive years.
people: With about 27,100 employees, each generates about $276K of revenue, 0.8x the Industrials median, and revenue has fallen 5.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $74K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.6M (13x revenue per employee).
